Content:
A line integral [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s] is similar to a definite integral, but for a function of multiple variables along a general path [MATH: C.]

Content:
To understand the intuition behind line integrals, remember that the definite integral [MATH: \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm{d}x] can be interpreted as the (signed) area bounded between the function [MATH: y=f(x)] and the [MATH: x]-axis between [MATH: x=a] and [MATH: x=b,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3c6fdce2a3288e801c01ac4ce119c98c]

Content:
Intuitively, we can think of the integral as the result of summing the areas of many small rectangles that we accumulate as we move along the [MATH: x]-axis on the path from [MATH: x=a] to [MATH: x=b.]

Content:
We can also draw paths as general curves in the plane. For example, consider the path [MATH: C,] given by
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle 2\cos t, 2\sin t \rangle, \qquad t\in \left[ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right].]
This path represents a quarter circle of radius [MATH: 2] traversed counterclockwise from [MATH: (2,0)] to [MATH: (0,2)] in the first quadrant:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6dbbd462015f5de04675d0a7ed332cb9]

Content:
Let [MATH: f(x,y)= 3 - \sin (2xy) .] If we sum the areas of the thin rectangles that are formed by the curve [MATH: C] and the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] as we move along the curve [MATH: C] from [MATH: (2,0)] to [MATH: (0,2),] we get a signed area, as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/231c3e48d4bfc54711e77357d5b32a1f]

Content:
This signed area is equal to the line integral [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s.]

Content:
Finally, we sometimes call [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s] as the line integral of [MATH: f] with respect to arc length. Other types of line integral are possible, as we'll see soon.

[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Here, we have [MATH: f(x,y) = xy^3]. Along the path, we have [MATH: x=\cos t] and [MATH: y=\sin t,] and so we get

[MATH: f(r(t))|= f(\cos t, \sin t); = \cos t ⋅ (\sin t)^{3}; = \sin^{3} t\cos t.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(\cos t)i + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)j; = − \sin ti + \cos tj; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt((− \sin t)^{2} + (\cos t)^{2}); = sqrt(\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t); = 1.]

[MATH: ∫_(C)xy^{3}ds|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}\sin^{3} t\cos t ⋅ 1dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}\sin^{3} t\cos tdt.]

So, we conclude that

[MATH: \int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s = \int^{\pi/2}_{0} \sin^3 t \cos t \, \textrm{d}t .]

[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Since [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j},] then along the curve we have [MATH: x=3t] and [MATH: y=4t.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get the following:

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(3t)i + (d)/(dt)(4t)j; = 3i + 4j; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt(3^{2} + 4^{2}); = sqrt(5^{2}); = 5]

Now, if [MATH: f(x,y) =xy,] then we obtain

[MATH: f(r(t))|= 3t ⋅ 4t; = 12t^{2}.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as

[MATH: ∫_(C)xyds|= ∫_{0}^{1}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}12t^{2} ⋅ 5dt; = 60∫_{0}^{1}t^{2}dt; = 60[(t^{3})/(3)]_{0}^{1}; = 20[t^{3}]_{0}^{1}; = 20.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A line integral [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s] is similar to a definite integral, but for a function of multiple variables along a general path [MATH: C.]

Content:
To understand the intuition behind line integrals, remember that the definite integral [MATH: \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm{d}x] can be interpreted as the (signed) area bounded between the function [MATH: y=f(x)] and the [MATH: x]-axis between [MATH: x=a] and [MATH: x=b,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3c6fdce2a3288e801c01ac4ce119c98c]

Content:
Intuitively, we can think of the integral as the result of summing the areas of many small rectangles that we accumulate as we move along the [MATH: x]-axis on the path from [MATH: x=a] to [MATH: x=b.]

Content:
We can also draw paths as general curves in the plane. For example, consider the path [MATH: C,] given by
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle 2\cos t, 2\sin t \rangle, \qquad t\in \left[ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right].]
This path represents a quarter circle of radius [MATH: 2] traversed counterclockwise from [MATH: (2,0)] to [MATH: (0,2)] in the first quadrant:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6dbbd462015f5de04675d0a7ed332cb9]

Content:
Let [MATH: f(x,y)= 3 - \sin (2xy) .] If we sum the areas of the thin rectangles that are formed by the curve [MATH: C] and the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] as we move along the curve [MATH: C] from [MATH: (2,0)] to [MATH: (0,2),] we get a signed area, as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/231c3e48d4bfc54711e77357d5b32a1f]

Content:
This signed area is equal to the line integral [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s.]

Content:
Finally, we sometimes call [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s] as the line integral of [MATH: f] with respect to arc length. Other types of line integral are possible, as we'll see soon.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The General Formula

Content:
Let [MATH: C] be a "smooth" curve, defined parametrically as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}(t), \qquad t \in (a,b).]
Now let [MATH: f(x,y)] be a continuous function that is defined everywhere on [MATH: C.] The line integral of [MATH: f] over [MATH: C,] denoted

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s,]

Content:
can be calculated using the formula

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Content:
The line integral formula extends to functions of [MATH: n] variables. For example, for functions of three variables, we can use the formula
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y,z) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Content:
We'll go through the details of where this formula comes from at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's get some practice at computing line integrals.

---

Item 3 — Example: Writing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function as a Definite Integral

Example Prompt:
Find an integral that is equivalent to [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s,] where [MATH: C] is the curve parametrized by [MATH: \mathbf r(t)= \left \langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle] for [MATH: t \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/02b83c814a778a787ec461430e53ac92]

The path of integration is shown above. We will use the formula

[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Here, we have [MATH: f(x,y) = xy^3]. Along the path, we have [MATH: x=\cos t] and [MATH: y=\sin t,] and so we get

[MATH: f(r(t))|= f(\cos t, \sin t); = \cos t ⋅ (\sin t)^{3}; = \sin^{3} t\cos t.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(\cos t)i + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)j; = − \sin ti + \cos tj; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt((− \sin t)^{2} + (\cos t)^{2}); = sqrt(\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t); = 1.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as

[MATH: ∫_(C)xy^{3}ds|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}\sin^{3} t\cos t ⋅ 1dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}\sin^{3} t\cos tdt.]

So, we conclude that

[MATH: \int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s = \int^{\pi/2}_{0} \sin^3 t \cos t \, \textrm{d}t .]

[MATH: \overline{P_0P_1} \cup \overline{P_1P_2} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{P_{n-1}P_n}.]

Content:
The width of each line segment is given by

Content:
[MATH: ||\overline{P_{k-1}P_k}|| .]

Content:
If [MATH: P_k] is at the tip of [MATH: \mathbf r(t_k),] then by the mean value theorem,

Content:
[MATH: ‖P_{k − 1}P_{k}^(―)‖|= ‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖(t_{k} − t_{k − 1}); = ‖r^{′}(c_{k})‖Δt_{k}]
for some intermediate point [MATH: c_k \in [t_{k-1}, t_k],] where [MATH: \Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}.]

Content:
Therefore, the area formed by the rectangle with a width of [MATH: \big\| \overline{P_{k-1}P_k} \big\|] and a height of [MATH: f(c_k)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: f(c_k) \| \mathbf r'(c_k)\|\Delta t_k.]

Content:
Step 3: We sum the areas of all of our small rectangles, which gives us an approximation of our line integral. We get

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s \approx \sum_{k=1}^{n} f(\mathbf r(c_k)) \| \mathbf{r}'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k.]
